papers.title: Characterisation of B-type stars in four young Galactic open clusters. II. Photometric variability with TESS and identification of pulsating stars
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27680v1

summary.one_liner: Photometric study with TESS full-frame images of 82 B-type stars in five young Galactic open clusters (h and chi Persei, NGC 457, NGC 581, NGC 1960), classifying pulsators and testing how pulsations and binarity relate.
summary.plain:
This paper looks at hot, massive young stars grouped together in star clusters about 15 to 30 million years old. The authors used images from NASA's TESS satellite, which records how stars brighten and dim over time, to extract light curves for 63 of 82 stars. Most of these stars show brightness changes caused by internal pulsations, and the team sorts them into pulsator types.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Pulsations inside massive stars affect their structure and evolution, so a clear census of which stars pulsate helps test models of them. The paper also reports that pulsations do not seem to hide most close companion stars from spectroscopic detection, with an exception for Be stars, which may need a higher velocity threshold; the wider significance of this is not established by the text alone.</plain>
<parameter name="background">- Open clusters: groups of stars born together from the same cloud, so they share roughly the same age and composition.
- B-type stars: hot, massive, blue-white stars; a few million to tens of millions of years of life.
- Pulsation: a star's surface swelling and shrinking periodically, seen as regular brightness changes.
- Beta Cephei stars: a class of B-type pulsators with fairly short pulsation periods.
- Be stars: B-type stars that show emission lines from a surrounding gas disc, often rapidly rotating.
- Light curve: a record of a star's brightness over time.
- Binary detection: companions are often found by measuring a star's radial velocity (motion toward or away from us) shifting over time; a threshold of about 20 km/s is the typical cutoff used.
- TESS: a space telescope surveying most of the sky for brightness changes.

papers.abstract: Pulsations and binarity are important properties of massive stars and influence their structure and evolution. Young open clusters are ideal laboratories to study massive stars, since they are mostly coeval and chemically homogeneous. We analyse 82 B-type stars in the Galactic open clusters $h$ and $\chi$ Persei, NGC 457, NGC 581, and NGC 1960, which have ages between 15 and 30 Myr. We extract light curves using both simple aperture photometry and a point-spread-function-based method that minimises contamination from crowded fields in full-frame images from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. We successfully extract light curves for 63 stars. The majority have photometric variability caused by pulsations, showing how pulsations are a common property of young B-type stars in clusters. We classify stars into different pulsator types based on their spectral type and frequency spectrum. The most common pulsator class are beta Cephei stars, with 29 stars in total, and we discover pulsation modes in almost all stars with a spectral type of B2 or earlier. All Be stars show pulsations, which supports the consensus of the ubiquity of pulsations in these stars. Finally, we confirm that the majority of early B-type stars are in binary systems, except for two pulsating Be stars and a star with rotational modulation. This indicates that pulsations do not significantly bias the spectroscopic detection of short-period binaries, except for Be stars where the spectroscopic radial velocity variability threshold should be higher than the typical value of 20 km s$^{-1}$.

papers.title: Accretor Luminosity as Probe of Orbital Evolution and Magnetic Braking in AM CVn Binaries
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26973v1

summary.one_liner: Models of AM CVn binaries show that the cooling luminosity of the accreting white dwarf, compared with observations, requires extra orbital angular momentum loss from magnetic braking of the donor, and that the Rappaport et al. 1983 and boosted Matt et al. 2015 prescriptions fit the data while the CARB formalism does not.
summary.plain: AM CVn binaries are pairs of stars so close together that a white dwarf (a dense, burnt-out star) steals helium-rich material from a companion, and their orbits slowly shrink or widen over time. The authors use how bright the white dwarf appears, since it reflects how hot and young it is, as a clock for that orbital change. They find that the observed brightness is best matched when the donor star loses extra spin by magnetic braking, but only if the standard formulas are scaled up by a large factor.
summary.why: The white dwarf's brightness gives a way to test how these binaries lose orbital energy, which is hard to measure directly. The paper also suggests that the widely used CARB braking formula is in tension with the data, and it motivates UV spectroscopy and new white dwarf atmosphere models; how well these conclusions hold depends on the modelling assumptions, which the summary text does not detail.
summary.background:
- AM CVn binaries: very compact systems (orbits under about 70 minutes) where a white dwarf accretes helium-rich matter from a small companion.
- Orbital period: the time for the two stars to complete one orbit; it changes as angular momentum is lost.
- Gravitational wave emission: the energy loss from orbiting masses that shrinks the orbit; it is the baseline model here.
- Magnetic braking: loss of angular momentum from a magnetised, wind-emitting star, which slows its spin and drags the orbit; several formulas exist (Rappaport 1983, Matt 2015, CARB).
- Accretor luminosity: the brightness of the accreting white dwarf, which depends on how much it has been heated by accretion and how long it has been cooling.
- Formation channels: the paper compares three evolutionary routes (white dwarf donor, helium star donor, evolved cataclysmic variable).

papers.abstract: AM CVn binaries are ultracompact systems with orbital periods $P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 70$ min, where a white dwarf accretes from a He-rich semidegenerate donor. At short orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 20$ min), rapid accretion reheats the accretor. As the system widens and the mass transfer rate decreases, the accretor follows standard white dwarf cooling at longer orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \gtrsim 30$ min). The accretor cooling luminosity then acts as a powerful probe into the orbital evolution of the binary. Recent observations show that the accretor appears brighter (younger) at long orbital periods, compared to models where orbital angular momentum loss is solely set by gravitational wave emission. We show that additional angular momentum loss, which we ascribe to magnetic braking of the donor, can better reproduce observations of accretor luminosity. We test and constrain various proposed magnetic braking formalisms, for the white dwarf, helium star, and evolved cataclysmic variable (CV) channels for AM CVn formation. None of the magnetic braking formalisms in their original form can reproduce the observations, but the widely popular magnetic braking proposed by Rappaport et al. 1983 boosted by a factor $\approx 5$, or the saturated magnetic braking proposed by Matt et al. 2015 boosted by a factor of $\approx 150$, yields satisfactory results. We also find that the CARB formalism, recently applied to the evolved CV channel, is strongly in tension with observations of accretor luminosity. Our models motivate UV spectroscopy observations, and dedicated WD atmosphere models for AM CVn accretors.

papers.title: Precise Radii of Visual Binaries with Dynamical Masses: $ξ$ Bootis $\&$ 70 Ophiuchi
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27031v1

summary.background:
- Binary star: two stars orbiting a common centre; a "visual" binary can be seen as two separate points in a telescope.
- Dynamical mass: mass found from the orbit using Newton's gravity, which is among the most direct mass measurements.
- Interferometry (CHARA Array): combining light from several telescopes to resolve the apparent angular size of a star.
- Angular diameter plus parallax (Gaia DR3 distance) gives the physical radius; bolometric flux plus radius gives effective temperature.
- Stellar evolutionary models (Lyon, Dartmouth, PARSEC, MIST): computer predictions of how a star's radius, temperature and brightness change with mass and age.
- Radius inflation: stars appearing larger than models predict, often linked to magnetic activity in close binaries.
- Eclipsing binary: a pair whose stars pass in front of each other, letting their sizes be measured from light curves.
- Coeval: formed at the same time.
summary.one_liner: Interferometric angular diameters, combined with dynamical masses and Gaia parallaxes, give radii and temperatures to about 2% for the two wide binaries ξ Bootis and 70 Ophiuchi, which are compared against four stellar evolution models and a set of short-period eclipsing binaries.
summary.plain: The paper studies two pairs of nearby Sun-like stars that orbit each other widely, so each star can be measured on its own. The authors used a telescope array to measure how large each star looks in the sky, then worked out their true sizes and surface temperatures. They found that these stars match four standard computer models of how stars age, while a separate group of close, tightly orbiting star pairs appears larger and often cooler than the models predict.
summary.why: Stellar models underpin much of astronomy, from ages of planets' host stars to exoplanet sizes, so checking them against stars with well-measured masses and sizes matters. The result suggests that tight binary orbits, rather than a star's age or mass alone, may be linked to the extra size seen in some stars; the text does not establish why this happens.

papers.abstract: A new orbital solution for $ξ$ Bootis (GJ 566 AB, P=152 yrs) and the recently revised orbital solution for 70 Ophiuchi (GJ 702 AB, P=88 yrs) yield component masses precise to 0.4\%. Their relatively wide separations ($>0.4^{\prime\prime}$) allow the components to be studied independently, making them ideal for testing the predictions of stellar evolutionary models. We use the six-telescope near-infrared MIRC-X and MYSTIC beam combiners at the CHARA Array to measure the angular diameters of all 4 stars. Combined with precise Gaia DR3 parallax values and bolometric fluxes, these interferometric measurements translate to stellar radii that are precise to $<2.4\%$ and effective temperatures precise to $<1.7\%$. We compare the measured radii and temperatures to four stellar evolutionary models (Lyon, Dartmouth, PARSEC, MIST). Over the mass range $0.67 - 0.91$ M$_\odot$, all models reproduce the observed properties within a few standard deviations, with no systematic offsets. The pairs are coeval and consistent with independent age estimates, further validating model predictions. With physical separations greater than 20 au, these pairs show no evidence of radius inflation, despite being spectroscopically classified as chromospherically active, and in the case of $ξ$ Bootis, probable members of the adolescent age ($\sim 0.4$ Gyr) Ursa Majoris Moving Group. In contrast, a set of 21 short-period ($P\lesssim$ 10 days) eclipsing binary stars with similar dynamical masses and metallicities are larger and often cooler than these same model predictions. Within this mass range, radius inflation appears to be associated with short-period binary star systems.

papers.title: Ultraviolet Observations of Solar Active Phenomena
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27071v1

summary.background:
- Ultraviolet (UV) light is invisible to the eye and is used to see the Sun's hot, thin outer layers.
- Chromosphere is the thin layer just above the Sun's visible surface; the corona is the much hotter outer atmosphere.
- Magnetic reconnection is when twisted magnetic field lines snap and reconnect, releasing energy as jets or flares.
- Coronal waves and dimmings (regions that temporarily look darker after an eruption) are used to infer the hidden magnetic field and the mass ejected.
- Elemental fractionation means the amounts of elements in the corona differ from those in the lower atmosphere, especially elements with low first ionization potential (the energy needed to strip their first electron).
- Type III radio bursts are fast radio emissions linked to electron beams travelling outward through the solar atmosphere.
summary.one_liner: This is a review-style overview of ultraviolet and extreme ultraviolet observations of solar activity, covering jets, flares, eruptions with their waves and dimmings, and elemental fractionation in the corona.
summary.plain: The paper surveys what ultraviolet telescopes have shown about the Sun's outer atmosphere, from the chromosphere up through the corona. It covers bursts such as jets, flares, and large eruptions that throw magnetized plasma into space. The text is a short summary and does not report specific new measurements or numbers.
summary.why: Solar activity is the closest case we can study in detail, and the authors suggest these results may help interpret activity on other stars that cannot be imaged directly. That link is stated as a belief in the text, not demonstrated here, so it should be read as a stated expectation rather than a proven result.

papers.abstract: Ultraviolet observations of the Sun have revolutionized our understanding of the structure and dynamics of the solar atmosphere. From the chromosphere all the way to the corona, there are ubiquitous jets due to magnetic reconnection and associated with type III radio bursts. Sporadic flares occur in the corona, representing an inevitable breakup of magnetic energy accumulation as new magnetic flux continues to pump into the solar atmosphere, which is further shuffled by solar surface motions. Once large-scale eruptions occur, magnetized plasmas are expelled out into the interplanetary space, leaving globally propagating waves and the following dimmings. The waves can be utilized to diagnose the coronal magnetic field which cannot be measured directly, and the dimmings can be used to estimate the ejected mass of eruptions and magnetic connectivity. Extreme ultraviolet spectroscopic observations provide information on the fractionation of different chemical elements, in particular those elements with low first ionization potential. Thanks to the high spatial resolution of solar observations, all these results are believed to shed light on our understanding of the activity on other stars which cannot be imaged.

papers.title: Sherlock 'Chrones: The Curious Case of NGC 6791 and Asteroseismic Targets Therein Reveals Mixing Length Dependence on Evolutionary Stage
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25306v1

summary.background:
- Isochrone: a theoretical curve showing where stars of one age and composition sit on a brightness-versus-colour diagram.
- Star cluster: a group of stars born together, so they share an age and starting composition; useful as a test bed.
- Mixing length (alpha_MLT): a tunable parameter in 1D stellar models describing how far rising hot gas travels in convection, expressed relative to the Sun's value.
- Convection: heat transport by churning motion of gas inside a star, which simple models can only approximate.
- Asteroseismology: studying stars by their vibrations, which gives precise measurements of their interiors and surface gravity (log g).
- Main sequence turn-off and red giant branch: the bend where stars leave the main sequence and the later phase of swollen, cooler giant stars.
- Metal-rich vs metal-poor: astronomers' term for stars with more or fewer elements heavier than helium.
summary.one_liner: Custom stellar isochrones with varying convective mixing length are fitted to the old open cluster NGC 6791 and globular cluster M92, finding the best-fit mixing length drops steadily along the evolutionary sequence, which challenges single-valued mixing-length calibrations.
summary.plain: This paper looks at groups of stars that all formed at the same time, using them as test cases for models of how stars age. The authors compared model tracks that use different values of a setting describing how hot gas churns inside stars, for an old open cluster (NGC 6791) and an old globular cluster (M92). They found the best-fitting setting changes as stars move from the turn-off point to the upper red giant branch, rather than staying constant.
summary.why: Most stellar models assume one fixed convection setting, calibrated on the Sun, and this work suggests that assumption may be too rigid, which could affect ages and properties derived from clusters. The text says the trend is consistent with predictions from more detailed 3D convection simulations, but the broader implications are not tested in the text.

papers.abstract: As single-aged populations containing stars spanning a range of masses but otherwise with similar properties, star clusters provide valuable testbeds for stellar evolution theory. The old, metal-rich, open cluster NGC 6791 is well studied, but the availability of asteroseismic observations of individual cluster members allows for a more in-depth analysis. Driven by mounting evidence that the solar assumption for convection used in almost all 1D stellar models is not adequate, and in light of the increased precision provided by modern data and asteroseismic constraints, we built and compared custom isochrones with varying values of the convective mixing length, $α_\text{MLT}$, to two clusters with well-determined ages: NGC 6791 and the well-studied, metal-poor globular cluster M92. For both clusters, we found that the best-fitting mixing length parameter decreases monotonically as a function of evolutionary phase, finding values between $0.98-1.10α_{\odot}$ for NGC 6791 and $1.16-1.21α_{\odot}$ for M92. In NGC 6791, this corresponds to an 18% decrease in the best fitting mixing length between the main sequence turn-off and upper end of the red giant branch. The degree of variation found within this one object is therefore comparable to variation across the literature in $α_\text{MLT}$ fits for other non-solar targets, calling single-valued $α_\text{MLT}$ fits to clusters into question. It is also consistent with $\log g$-$α_\text{MLT}$ trends predicted by higher-fidelity, 3D convection analyses. Our results therefore illustrate the need for more flexibility in our treatment of the mixing length in isochrones to properly model clusters.

papers.title: 3D Binary Evolution of a Merging Binary Black Hole Progenitor
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25310v1

summary.background:
- Binary star: two stars orbiting each other; one can pull gas off the other through mass transfer.
- Black hole merger: two compact remnants spiral together and emit gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime.
- Case A/B/C mass transfer: labels for when in its life the donor star overflows its boundary (Case B means after core hydrogen runs out, during shell burning).
- Roche lobe and Lagrange points: the teardrop-shaped region around each star where gravity is dominated by that star; L2 and L3 are points outside it where gas can escape.
- Hydrodynamics: computer modeling of how fluids (here, stellar gas) flow and push.
- Metallicity: the fraction of elements heavier than helium in a star; low metallicity stars lose less mass to winds.
- MESA: a widely used open-source 1D stellar evolution code.
- Equipotential/hydrostatic equilibrium: the gas is assumed to sit in balance under gravity and pressure.
summary.one_liner: A 3D hydrodynamics model, coupled to the MESA stellar evolution code via the shellular approximation and time-incremented multiscale evolution, follows mass transfer in a likely merging binary black hole progenitor (30 Msun donor, 9.3 Msun black hole, low metallicity) through two Case B mass-transfer phases and compares it with the 1D Kolb & Ritter (1990) prescription.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a pair of stars in which a massive star is slowly feeding gas onto a black hole that orbits it. Such pairs are thought to be the ancestors of black hole mergers that send gravitational waves through space. The authors simulated this exchange in full 3D, alternating between a stellar evolution model and a fluid-flow model, from the end of the star's main life until its core runs out of carbon.
summary.why: Mass transfer between stars is a key step in making merging black hole pairs, but simpler 1D models have to approximate it. The text reports that the 3D run matched a standard 1D prescription closely except at one stage, that the gas did not spill past the outer balance point (L3) as 1D models predicted, and that merger timing was not significantly changed. The authors also suggest the outflows could matter for X-ray observations, though the text does not show that directly.

papers.abstract: Mass transfer is a highly dynamical 3D process that spans evolutionary timescales in binary stars. It is key to the production of gravitational waves through formation of binary black holes and other double compact objects. We integrate global 3D hydrodynamics into stellar evolutionary modeling to resolve mass transfer across nuclear timescales. We employ the shellular approximation in the stellar evolution code MESA to map a 3D spatial structure by equipotential shells in the Roche geometry to maintain hydrostatic equilibrium across tidally-distorted surfaces. We employ the method of time-incremented multiscale evolution to alternate between stellar evolution and 3D hydrodynamics to span large timescales with dynamical feedback. We employ this framework to examine a likely merging binary black hole progenitor system of a low-metallicity 30Msol donor star and 9.3Msol black hole from the end of the main sequence to core Carbon depletion. We modeled two complete mass transfer phases in 3D while self-consistently accounting for stellar evolution. These comprised a thermal-timescale early Case B phase and a nuclear-timescale late Case B phase. The prescription of Kolb & Ritter (1990) closely predicted the results of 3D evolution, except at the end of the first phase of mass transfer; our 3D model remained well-contained by the outer Lagrange point, despite 1D predictions of substantial L3 overflow during this stage. We find incorporating 3D hydrodynamics during Case B mass transfer did not significantly impact expected merger times. Our model never overflowed L3 as predicted by 1D prescriptions. L2/L3 outflows formed even while underflowing those equipotentials. Our model suggests these outflows can be neglected for the evolution of similar systems, but were dense enough to potentially impact X-ray observations.

papers.title: Sun-like stars show lowered X-ray activity together with over-rotation at beyond-solar ages
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24459v1

summary.background:
- Stellar age-rotation relation (Skumanich law): older sun-like stars spin more slowly, roughly with a simple power law of age.
- Magnetic braking: a star's magnetised wind carries away angular momentum, slowing its spin.
- Coronal X-ray emission: a star's hot outer atmosphere glows in X-rays, driven by magnetic dynamo activity; it is used as a proxy for magnetic activity.
- Asteroseismology: measuring stellar oscillations (vibrations) to estimate a star's internal structure and age.
- M67: an open cluster of about 4 billion years used as a benchmark for stellar rotation.
- Metallicity ([Fe/H]): the abundance of iron relative to the Sun, used as a proxy for a star's chemical composition.
summary.one_liner: Using deep XMM-Newton X-ray observations and asteroseismic ages, this paper finds that older, slightly more massive sun-like stars are unusually X-ray dim and rotate faster than expected for their age, and discusses inefficient spin-down as a possible cause.
summary.plain: Stars like the Sun slow their spin as they age, and their X-ray glow is tied to that spin. This paper looks at a set of older sun-like stars whose ages were measured by listening to their vibrations, and checks how bright they are in X-rays. The slightly more massive early-G and late-F stars appear dimmer in X-rays than their spin would predict, and they spin faster than similar-coloured stars in the cluster M67, even though they are older.
summary.why: It suggests that the usual rule linking a star's age, spin and magnetic activity may not hold for all sun-like stars, which matters for estimating stellar ages from rotation. The authors offer hampered angular momentum loss as a possible cause, but the text presents this as an argument rather than a settled explanation, and it conflicts with M67 studies.

papers.abstract: In recent years, substructure in the age-rotation relationship of cool, sun-like stars has been identified, showing deviations from the historical Skumanich law. Since magnetic activity is expected to be the physical root cause of the stellar spin-down, namely via the magnetic braking process mediated through stellar winds, changes in spin-down should correspond to unusual activity behaviour. We selected a sample of old sun-like stars in the solar neighborhood with asteroseismic age estimates and measured rotation periods, and present an analysis of their magnetic activity using deep X-ray observations from XMM-Newton. We observe that sample stars less massive than the Sun (late-G and early-K) agree well with the established rotation-activity relationship, while early-G and late-F stars with masses above solar tend to be unusually X-ray dim for their rotation period. The latter stars rotate faster than same-colour stars in the solar-age open cluster M67, despite being older than M67. Those stars are characterized by either low metallicity ([Fe/H]$\approx -0.2$ dex compared to solar) or by a mix of low coronal temperatures ($< 1.5$ million K) and very low X-ray surface fluxes ($\lesssim 10^4$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$). We conclude that there is sufficient dynamo activity for coronal emission in the sample stars, since we successfully detect the majority of them in our X-ray observations. We argue that stars with extremely low coronal temperature and/or low X-ray flux through the stellar surface may produce an inefficient spin-down through hampered angular momentum shedding. If this is indeed the cause for their over-rotation, the onset age of this effect would need to be at an age of approximately 3~Gyr. However, this behaviour is at odds with studies of stars in the open cluster M67 with a cluster age of $\sim4$ Gyr, which do not show a faster-rotating population of sun-like stars.

papers.title: Asteroseismology of AI Velorum: a prototype of high-amplitude delta Scuti stars
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24796v1

summary.background:
- Delta Scuti stars: pulsating stars somewhat more massive than the Sun that brighten and dim periodically.
- High-amplitude (HADS) variants: pulsate with large brightness swings.
- Asteroseismology: inferring a star's interior structure from its pulsation frequencies, similar to inferring a drum's shape from its sound.
- Radial vs non-radial modes: radial modes swell and shrink the whole star; non-radial modes form patterns of surface motion.
- Opacity: a measure of how opaque stellar gas is to radiation; different tabulations (OPAL, OP, OPLIB) give different model predictions.
- Mixing-length parameter: a tunable value describing how efficiently convection (rising and sinking hot gas) carries energy.
- Convective core overshooting: convective mixing extending slightly beyond the core's nominal boundary.
- Hertzsprung-Russell diagram: a plot of stellar luminosity against temperature used to place stars by evolutionary stage.
- TESS: a NASA space telescope that measures starlight over long periods.
summary.one_liner: A detailed asteroseismic study of AI Velorum, a prototype high-amplitude delta Scuti pulsator, combining TESS photometry, Strömgren photometry and HARPS spectroscopy to fit stellar models and test three opacity datasets (OPAL, OP, OPLIB), convection efficiency and core overshooting.
summary.plain: AI Velorum is a star that pulses in brightness in several rhythms at once, and these rhythms carry information about its interior, somewhat like how an instrument's sound reveals its shape. The authors used satellite light measurements, ground-based colour measurements and detailed spectra to work out the star's basic properties, its age and its stage of life. They then compared computer models of the star against the observed pulsation frequencies and its position on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, a standard chart of star brightness versus temperature.
summary.why: The paper is a case study of one well-observed star, so its results apply most directly to this object and similar pulsators. It bears on how stellar models are calibrated, since the choice of opacity data (how readily stellar material blocks radiation) changes the predicted position of the star, and the authors note their preference for OPAL does not show that OPAL is generally better.

papers.abstract: AI Velorum is exceptional among high-amplitude δScuti (HADS) stars because of its multimode pulsations. Despite being an excellent target for asteroseismology, this prototype star has not been studied in detail. We determine the stellar parameters, age, and evolutionary stage of AI Vel, constrain envelope convection and convective core overshooting, and test three opacity data sets: OPAL, OP, and OPLIB. We analysed TESS photometry, ground-based Strömgren photometry, and HARPS spectroscopy. Modes were identified using photometric and spectroscopic methods, and empirical values of the non-adiabatic f-parameter were derived for both radial modes. Seismic modelling was performed within a Bayesian framework supported by Monte Carlo simulations. We confirm the radial nature of the two dominant modes and identify one non-radial mode as most likely an axisymmetric dipole or quadrupole mode. Within the explored parameter space, only OPAL models reproduce the observed position of AI Vel in the HR diagram, whereas OP and OPLIB models are too cool and underluminous. All seismic models favour inefficient envelope convection (mixing-length parameter alpha_{mlt}\lesssim 0.5). Including the non-radial mode substantially reduces the formal posterior uncertainties, but the ambiguity in its identification introduces additional model-dependent uncertainties. AI Vel is an evolved, slowly rotating star in the hydrogen shell-burning phase. Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of combining pulsation frequencies with empirical f-parameters. The preference for OPAL opacities is consistent with results for several other HADS and SX Phoenicis stars but does not imply a general superiority of OPAL opacities.

papers.title: Resolving Individual Massive Stars in an M31 Star Cluster Exhibiting Wolf-Rayet Features
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22375v1

summary.background:
- Massive stars: very heavy, hot stars that live short lives and often end as supernovae.
- Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars: a late, evolved phase of massive stars that has lost its outer layers; WC and WN are two subtypes distinguished by their chemical signatures in the spectrum.
- OB stars: hot, blue, young massive stars; yellow supergiants are a cooler, later evolutionary stage.
- M31 (Andromeda): our nearest large neighbouring galaxy, a common target for studying stellar populations from outside the Milky Way.
- LAMOST: a Chinese wide-field spectroscopic survey telescope; its fibre aperture (3.3 arcseconds here) collects light from a wide patch, so nearby stars blend together.
- HST (Hubble Space Telescope): its sharper imaging resolves stars that ground telescopes see as one blob. F275W is an ultraviolet filter.
- Contamination: light from unrelated nearby stars that leaks into a measurement and makes a star look different than it is.
summary.one_liner: Using HST imaging to resolve individual stars in a young, LAMOST-discovered cluster in M31 that shows Wolf-Rayet features, and quantifying how much crowding contaminates Wolf-Rayet photometry at HST and LAMOST scales.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a tight group of young stars in the Andromeda galaxy that shows the spectral signature of Wolf-Rayet stars, which are very hot, stripped-down massive stars. Ground-based telescopes blur such crowded groups together, so the authors used sharper space-telescope images to pick out the individual stars. They identified four Wolf-Rayet candidates, four hot OB-type stars and one yellow supergiant in the cluster.
summary.why: The observed ratio of two Wolf-Rayet subtypes (WC/WN) in Andromeda is higher than standard stellar evolution models predict, and the authors argue that contamination from neighbouring stars in crowded regions may be part of the reason the census is incomplete. The text says the approach could eventually give a contamination-corrected WC/WN ratio, but it does not say whether that will resolve the tension with models.

papers.abstract: The observed ratio of Wolf-Rayet (WR) star subtypes (e.g., WC/WN) in M31 is significantly higher than the predictions of standard stellar evolution models, yet this key diagnostic discrepancy remains unresolved. This is partly due to incomplete census and the challenge of resolving individual stars in compact clusters with ground-based telescopes. In this work, we report a young cluster with WR features with the (R.A., Dec) = (00:43:39.36, +41:10:08.7), discovered with LAMOST spectra. We use the high spatial resolution of the HST imaging data to resolve the cluster members, leading to the identification of four WR star candidates, four OB stars, and one yellow supergiant. Based on the current known WR sample in M31 observed in the HST F275W filter, about one-third of WRs are contaminated by other sources within a 1. "1 $\times$ 1. "1 aperture, while this fraction can reach up to two-thirds for the LAMOST fiber size of 3. "3. Applying the approach demonstrated in this work to a larger sample of crowded regions in M31 will yield a more complete census and allow for the measurement of a definitive WC/WN ratio, corrected for contamination. Whether this refined ratio increases or decreases the current tension with models remains to be seen, but it will provide the essential observational constraint needed to advance our understanding.

papers.title: A comprehensive Sun-as-a-star catalog of interplanetary type-III bursts: Statistics and a framework for stellar exospace weather applications
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22606v1

summary.background:
- Type-III radio bursts: brief radio emission made by fast electron beams travelling outward from the Sun through interplanetary space.
- Decameter-hectometric (DH): the wavelength/frequency range, roughly tens to hundreds of metres in wavelength, where these bursts are seen from spacecraft.
- Soft X-ray (SXR) flares: sudden brightenings of the Sun in X-rays; C5-class is a moderate flare strength on the standard scale.
- Coronal mass ejections (CMEs): large clouds of magnetised plasma thrown out from the Sun.
- Solar energetic particle events (SEPEs): bursts of high-energy protons and electrons reaching near-Earth space.
- Shock-associated (S-type) bursts: type-III bursts that coincide with a DH type-II burst, a signature of a shock wave moving outward.
- Logistic regression: a standard statistical method that gives the probability of a yes/no outcome from several inputs.
- Sun-as-a-star: treating the Sun as if it were a distant star, observing only its integrated signal.
summary.one_liner: A catalog of 538 Sun-as-a-star decameter-hectometric type-III radio bursts linked to C5+ flares (2006–2025), plus logistic-regression and scale-free models that use these bursts with soft X-ray flare data to estimate the odds of coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particle events, and a catalog of 26 shock-associated type-III bursts.
summary.plain: Solar flares can throw out fast electron beams, which make radio bursts that travel out through space. This paper builds a large list of such radio bursts from 2006 to 2025 and asks whether they help forecast which flares will be followed by dangerous eruptions of material or high-energy particles. The authors report that combining the radio information with the X-ray strength of the flare gives more accurate and better-calibrated predictions than using X-ray data alone.
summary.why: The idea is that the same radio signatures could one day help assess space weather around other stars, where we cannot directly measure particles or eruptions. This link to stellar flares is a proposal in the text rather than something tested here, so it should be read as a possibility.

papers.abstract: Decameter-hectometric (DH) type-III bursts, produced by energetic electron beams escaping into interplanetary (IP) space, are often associated with strong soft X-ray (SXR) flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and solar energetic particle events (SEPEs). With future DH missions being planned, these intense bursts could provide reliable exospace weather event diagnostics, given the lack of direct stellar IP particle and CME probes. We present a catalog of DH type-III bursts associated with 538 out of 734 $\geq$C5-class flares observed by Wind and STEREO spacecraft during 2006-2025. Independent of the SXR flare strength, the occurrence and Sun-as-a-star emission properties of DH type-III bursts distinguish confined flares, CMEs with and without strong IP shocks, and SEPEs. We find that logistic-regression models combining SXR and type-III properties provide more accurate and well-calibrated CME/SEPE occurrence probabilities than a model based only on SXR parameters. Further, a space weather event probability-estimation model based on physically meaningful, scale-free parameters derived from SXR and type-III properties outperforms an SXR parameter-only model. This result presents a way to define solar-calibrated exospace weather prediction models extendable to stellar flares with a range of energy scales but similar underlying physics. We also present a catalog of 26 shock-associated type-III (S-type-III) bursts that appear to start from cotemporal DH type-II bursts and are generally associated with fast halo CMEs and major SEPEs. Our catalogs and the scale-free model form a benchmark for exospace weather studies.

papers.title: The Stability Frontier of Interacting Binary Stars
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19026v1

summary.background:
- Binary star: two stars orbiting a common centre of mass.
- Roche overflow: when a star swells enough to spill gas onto its companion, through the gravitational boundary (Roche lobe) around each star.
- Accretion: gas falling onto a star.
- White dwarf: a small, dense stellar remnant about the size of Earth.
- Angular momentum and spin: the rotational "spin" of an object and the orbital motion both carry angular momentum, which must be conserved overall.
- Stability (dynamical): whether a small disturbance dies away (stable) or grows (unstable).
- Fold and oscillatory thresholds: a fold is where a steady state stops existing or changes character; an oscillatory threshold is where small disturbances start to swing back and forth.
- Gravitational waves: ripples in spacetime emitted by orbiting masses; the millihertz band is a range of wave frequencies targeted by planned space detectors.
- Orbital period derivative: how fast the orbital period is lengthening or shortening, measured by timing observations.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives a conservation-based stability boundary for interacting binary stars, applies it to conservative white dwarf binaries with direct impact accretion, and examines equilibrium fold, oscillatory, and synchronization-induced thresholds.
summary.plain: The paper asks when a pair of stars orbiting each other, where one feeds gas onto the other, will settle into a steady exchange of mass or will drift away from that state. The authors work through this for pairs of white dwarfs, the dense leftover cores of small stars, using conservation of mass, angular momentum and energy. They report the conditions under which a steady state is stable and where the system can instead start to oscillate.
summary.why: Interacting white dwarf pairs are candidate sources of millihertz gravitational waves, so stability limits bear on how such systems evolve and what detectors might see. The abstract says the calculated orbital period changes are consistent with published timing measurements within stated uncertainties, but the text provides no further detail on that comparison, so its strength is hard to judge from this summary alone.

papers.abstract: We derive a conservation based dynamical stability frontier for interacting binary stars that distinguishes stationary mass transfer from the restoration of a perturbed contact state. We apply the formalism to conservative white dwarf binaries with direct impact accretion, coupling Roche overflow, stream angular momentum, gravitational radiation, and both stellar spin reservoirs. From the contact equations, we obtain the required orbital return torque, and an exact Jacobian identity yields the restoring gradient and an oscillatory stability boundary in the computed white dwarf domain. A dimensionally normalized quadrupolar tide reveals separate equilibrium fold and oscillatory thresholds, including coexisting stable and unstable stationary branches. Finite donor synchronization introduces an additional oscillatory stability frontier. The model recovers the classical Roche and gravitational radiation limits, while the calculated orbital period derivatives are consistent with published binary timing measurements within their combined observational and model uncertainties. These results specify the torque amplitude, restoring stiffness, and synchronization rate needed for local stability, providing quantitative targets for stellar tidal calculations and the interpretation of interacting binaries in the millihertz gravitational wave band.

papers.title: XRISM/Xtend detection of solar wind charge exchange induced by multiple coronal mass ejections in 2024 August
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20934v1

summary.background:
- Solar wind: a continuous stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun.
- Coronal mass ejection (CME): a large burst of magnetised gas thrown from the Sun's outer atmosphere, sometimes after a solar flare.
- Solar wind charge exchange (SWCX): when highly charged ions in the solar wind capture electrons from neutral gas, they emit X-rays; this is a known part of the faint X-ray background seen near Earth.
- Emission lines: sharp bright X-ray wavelengths that act like fingerprints identifying specific elements and their ionization states.
- Ionization temperature: an effective temperature describing how stripped of electrons the ions are, which hints at the conditions where the gas was heated.
- Abundance and inverse-FIP pattern: how much of each element is present relative to others; the first ionization potential (FIP) effect is a known pattern in which low-FIP elements are enhanced in the corona, and an inverse pattern is the opposite.
- XRISM: a Japanese-led X-ray space observatory; Xtend is its wide-field X-ray imaging instrument.
- ACE: a NASA spacecraft at a point between Earth and the Sun that measures solar wind in situ.
- AtomDB: a public atomic database used to model X-ray emission from plasmas.
summary.one_liner: Using the XRISM/Xtend X-ray imager, the authors analyse a solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) X-ray enhancement during multiple coronal mass ejections in August 2024, fitting emission lines from C, N, O, Ne, Mg, Si and Fe and modelling ionization temperatures and abundances with AtomDB.
summary.plain: The Sun regularly throws out clouds of charged gas, called coronal mass ejections, and when this gas collides with neutral atoms near Earth it glows in X-rays. This paper looks at one such glow observed over five days in August 2024, when several solar flares and clouds hit at once. By splitting the X-ray light into its characteristic colours (spectral lines), the authors identified the elements present and estimated how hot the gas was when it left the Sun.
summary.why: The Sun's charged gas is hard to measure directly with spacecraft for some heavy elements, so reading it from X-ray glow could give a complementary view of the Sun's corona and of how solar eruptions differ in strength. The text reports that the ionization temperatures rose with flare intensity and were lower than typical flare temperatures, but the link to coronal heating and the composition patterns are suggestive interpretations from a single event that would need further checks.

papers.abstract: Solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) emission is often a major component of the soft X-ray background, but it also provides a remote diagnostic of the composition and ionization state of solar wind plasma. We present an analysis of a SWCX event observed with XRISM/Xtend during 2024 August 9-13. The event occurred during intense solar activity with multiple flares, including an X1.3-class solar flare, and associated coronal mass ejections (CMEs). We found a clear enhancement in the 0.3-3.0 keV count rate that occurred nearly simultaneously with an increase in the solar wind proton flux measured by ACE. We fitted the spectrum during the enhancement period with a set of Gaussian emission lines. In addition to the commonly detected C, N, and O lines, we detected Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe lines at $>15σ$ significance. We extracted two characteristic periods within the enhanced interval based on the CME arrival timeline. The O$_{\rm VIII}$/Si$_{\rm XIII}$ line ratio changed significantly between the two periods, suggesting contributions from multiple CME components. We then applied the AtomDB charge exchange model with a multi-temperature setup. The estimated ionization temperatures for Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe increased with the peak soft X-ray flux of the associated solar flares. This trend suggests that coronal heating becomes more efficient for more intense flares. Meanwhile, the ionization temperatures were lower than typical flare electron temperatures, implying that CME plasma may have been released into interplanetary space under non-equilibrium ionization conditions. We also found an indication of an inverse-FIP pattern, with reduced relative abundances of Si and S. These results demonstrate that XRISM/Xtend can diagnose the coronal plasma through SWCX emission, including heavy ions such as Ne, Mg, and Si, which are difficult to measure with current in-situ instruments (e.g., ACE satellite).
